On the order:
First reading of bill to amend the Civil Service Act (Director of Public Service)-Mr. Campbell.

This bill provides for the appointment of a director of civil service whose duty it shall be to co-ordinate the staffs of the various departments.
As such an appointment would involve an expenditure of money, the bill must receive the recommendation of the crown before it can be entertained by the house. Section 54 of the British North America Act provides that it shall not be lawful for the house to adopt any bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue to any purpose that has not first been recommended by message of the Governor General and our standing order No. 60 states that all motions made for charges upon the people must be first referred to the committee of the whole before any resolution of the house do pass thereupon.
It seems therefore that the bill cannot be introduced by a private member. I kftow that I allowed it last session when the hon. member gave very little explanation on introducing it, but I should certainly have ruled jt out of order had it come up for second reading. I therefore rule that the present motion is out of order.

The house resumed from Thursday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that, due to a railway tie-up on account of storms on the Canadian National railway between Montreal and Nova Scotia, I was not able to be present at the opening or to hear the mover and seconder of the address, I had occasion to read their speeches in Hansard and I think, with those who have preceded me in this debate, I can very sincerely tender my congratulations to those hon. gentlemen. Perhaps, I can go a step further with respect to the mover of the address, and say that the government of this country is to be congratulated upon paying a tribute to the province of Nova Scotia by selecting the mover of the address from that little province by the sea. I am sure the province will appreciate the honour and will also acknowledge that the mover of the address worthily upheld the capabilities of those coming from there.

The Address-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that I need pay attention in any specific way to the speech from the throne. It has been referred to by all those who have spoken as being of an empty character. I think it might be said that it was a Skilfully prepared document, closely and scrupulously evading anything of importance to the Dominion of Canada, and it probably will go down in history as a state document which would take first prize in respect of what it does not contain rather than for what it does contain.
I should like to make reference to the fact that the national fuel and steel question was omitted from the speech from the throne. The hon. member from Bow River (Mr. Garland) referred to this fact in his address yesterday, and made it clear that this matter has been long delayed by the parliament of this country. Definite action is an urgent necessity and the question should be taken into earnest consideration without further delay. I was pleased, Mr. Speaker, to hear the statement in the house to-day from the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) with respect to information received by me that Canadian government boats were being fueled with American coal at the port of Halifax. Yesterday afternoon I attempted to ask the question in the house and Your Honour ruled it out of order for what was probably a very good reason. The telegram I read to the house yesterday was followed by another telegram received by me last evening, and I am going to crave the indulgence of the house to read this second telegram now. The statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is very refreshing to us and I am sure will be appreciated by all those who live in Nova Scotia. The last telegram I received reads as follows:
Suggest you raise in house question of authenticity of following statement which appears in Evening Mail Thursday February second:
"Unemployment conditions are serious in sections of the mining centres of Cape Breton; Workmen are idle, women and children are in want of food and clothing. The situation is due to the fact that there are not sufficient coal sales during the winter months to keep the Nova Scotia mines operating at full time. In the meantime on the Halifax waterfront to-day two Canadian government ships the Arleux and the Lady Laurier are having their bunkers filled with United States coal-coal mined by United States workmen and brought to the capital city of one of the greatest coal mining provinces in the world. Was there ever a greater outrage, was there ever a greater sham than the slogan of the politicians, 'Canada for Canadians' "?
If that report is true, Mr. Speaker-and 1 have no reason to doubt it-it seems to me that, as stated in the telegram, the slogan, " Canada for Canadians," is certainly a sham [Mr. R. K. Smith.}
of the worst character. The coal districts in Nova Scotia are in a very bad condition at the present time as far as employment is concerned. In the isle of Cape Breton, which is part of the province, thousands of workmen are idle and their families are in destitute circumstances, due to the fact that the operators cannot find a ready market for their coal at this season of the year. And yet boats owned and operated by the government of this country are being fueled with American coal at the port of Halifax! It seems to me that immediate steps should be taken not only to ascertain whether this is being done, but, if such is the fact, to have the practice cease without any delay, because as long as it is allowed to continue-and I understand that it has been going on since 1921-you will lose entirely the respect of the people of Nova Scotia. And let it be remembered that one-fifth of the population of that province is directly dependent upon the coal and steel industry. Therefore any action that tends to prevent employment being secured by the miners of Nova Scotia is deeply resented by all.
Now, with respect to the coal industry in Nova Scotia, let me remind the House that this is not a new question. In 1924 a delegation came to Ottawa headed by the then premier of the province, the Hon. Mr. Armstrong. That delegation presented their views and their claims to the government of the day and in no uncertain terms stated that unless some immediate steps were taken to remedy the then deplorable situation in the coal fields of the province calamitous results would follow. After that, Mr. Speaker, came the recommendation in an addendum to the report submitted to the provincial government by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan-not the Dominion Duncan report, but the provincial. In that addendum Mr. Cronyn, one of the commissioners, recommended to the government of Canada that this industry be placed on some sort of stable basis, insisting that it needed more tariff protection in order to compete with imported coal. I should like to say, sir, that this recommendation was not taken seriously by the government.
Then came the famous Duncan report that was submitted to this parliament last session. In that report by implication, if not expressly, we were told that the tariff on ooal was not sufficient. Those are not the exact words; the language used was something like this-that the question of the tariff on coal should receive' the immediate attention of the tariff advisory board, and they recommended that it be placed before that board without

The . Address-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
delay. Well, the subject could not logically be placed before the tariff board for any reduction in duty; the duty is far too low now; it could only be placed before the tariff board for a substantial increase in duty. So I say the question of the coal industry, so far as the east is concerned, has been completely neglected by this government, and no effort has been made to see that it takes its proper place as one of the greatest basic industries of the Dominion.
It is not difficult to discover what the policies of the different parties in the Dominion are with respect to the coal industry. I have before me the remarks of the Liberal candidate who was contesting the county of Cumberland in 1921. Addressing a meeting at Amherst on October 5, in the presence of the Prime Minister, who was then the leader of the opposition, the Liberal candidate said:
Free trade is not the policy of the Liberal party. If it were I would oppose it because I believe it would briug disaster to our industries and remove from the farmers the home market which is practically the only market they have left. Free trade may be all right from the wealthy grain growers of the west whose wheat goes to the foreign markets and who do not have to worry about selling their produce at home, but it would mean paralysis in the maritime provinces. Also, I am a firm believer in the establishment of a national coal policy for Canada-no country, especially a country with cold winters, which depends on a foreign nation for its fuel, can claim to be independent of that nation.
Then he announced his policy:
Every pound of coal purchased by the government should be mined by Canadian miners and transported over government railways to the points of consumption. Coal required by other consumers in Canada should be carried at cost.
This is reported in the Halifax Chronicle of October 6, 1921. As I have said, on the platform at the time was the present Prime Minister of this Dominion. Therefore, I take it, Mr. Speaker, that so far as the coal industry of Nova Scotia is concerned that was the Liberal policy in 1921.

Now, Mr
Speaker, if that was the policy of the Liberal party in 1921, certainly no effort has been made on their part to carry it into effect. Such a policy is certainly needed. Unless something is done, as Mr. Cronyn has pointed out, we can only expect a calamitous situation in the coal fields of Nova Scotia. The royalties on coal are one of the principal sources of revenue for the province, and consequently when the coal industry is stagnant the provincial revenues are correspondingly depleted. If the coal industry is in a flourishing condition it benefits generally the whole province; but I am sorry to say that the industry is not flourishing to-day, but the reverse of that.
What we need, Mr. Speaker, is a national fuel and steel policy, and I believe that the following measures would help to bring this policy about. In the first place, coking plants should be established. Some attention was given to this last session, and I believe something is being done along these lines at the present time.	*

What about the use of
Canadian coal?

I was told quite recently that a plant is being established in the city of Montreal which is to use four hundred tons of coal a day in the manufacture of coke, but that the coal is to be American coal. I am not sure whether that is correct.
Correct.

Then it is
a crying shame that that sort of thing should be allowed to go on. Yesterday the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) drew attention to the value of the coal fields in the province of Alberta, and stated that those deposits were greater than all the coal deposits in the other parts of the British Empire. It is inconceivable that in a country like Canada, striving to get on its feet economically, and claiming by some to have reached the status of a nation, American coal should be allowed to come in at the expense of our own coal miners and coal operators and to the great disadvantage of certain parts of the Dominion. Has it ever occurred to hon. members that an emergency might arise in this country Whereby we might be shut off from securing coal in the United States or other parts of the world? The United States is the country from which we secure most of our imported bituminous coal, and a crisis might arise at any time whereby our supply from that market would be entirely shut off, and we would be thrown back upon our own resources, and possibly not be able to cope with the demands that would be made upon our own supplies. It seems to me that we must look at this situation from the viewpoint of national development,
152	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
from the viewpoint of saving and safeguarding those industries which are of such great benefit to this country, and unless we do inaugurate and put into force a policy of that character, it seems to me that we shall never truly be able to say that we have reached a state of nationhood.
I was going on to mention the different factors that occurred to me as necessary in the building up of a national steel and fuel policy:	First, the establishment of
coking plants; second, a subvention granting assistance in the carrying of coal west of Montreal; third, real tariff consideration against importations of coke, anthracite screenings and bituminous coal; fourth, more favourable transportation rates; and fifth, the abolition of the customs drawback on foreign coals used in coking.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if these methods were inaugurated, we would make an effective start at all events at putting Canada on the basis of securing a national fuel policy which I believe would work out in the end to the advantage of every section of the country, because if we doubled the output of coal in the Dominion, doubled the output of the coal fields of Alberta and Nova Scotia, we must naturally expect that there would be a reduction in the price to the consumer; that is the natural consequence that we must expect to follow, that with the output, doubled, there would be a corresponding decrease in price to the consumer.
I come now to the question of subsidies, as outlined in the Duncan report submitted to this house last year. I am not so sure but that not only the government of this country, but parliament also, missed not only the spirit of the Duncan report but the phraseology as well with respect to provincial subsidies. I would like to read a short paragraph from the Duncan report in this connection. The report says, on page 19:
We do not feel, however, that it would be right or wise that the maritime provinces, in their present state of grave necessity, with deficits accumulating against them in their ordinary revenue and expenditure, should be left in suspense until a reassessment is made by the Dominion government, and accordingly we recommend that immediate interim lumpsum increases should be made in the payments to the three maritime provinces as follows:-
The report then goes on to enumerate the payments-$875,000 to Nova Scotia, and so on. I would call the attention of the house to the words used by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan in this report. He says, "immediate interim lump-sum increase." The report was filed with the government of the day on
[Mr. R. K. Smith.)
September 23, 1926, and the first instalment of the subsidies was paid in July, 1927. At that time only one-half of the $875,000 was sent to the province of Nova Scotia. The balance was held by the Dominion treasury until late in November, until, as a matter of fact, after the Dominion-provincial conference held in Ottawa last fall, at which, representatives of our province brought the question up and forced the hands of the Minister of Finance to send along the balance of the subsidy, which should have been sent to us in July. Not only that, but even then the sum of $133,000 was held back from the final payment owing to a disputed claim between the province and the federal government in connection with the sending of the militia to the island of Cape Breton. That sum of $133,000 was deducted from the subsidy. The province of Nova Scotia disputes this claim. It is out of all proportion to the services rendered, and I claim that the federal government had no right and no authority whatsoever for withholding this amount from the subsidy that was sent to M)va Scotia. It is quite true that under the Militia Act there are certain regulations whereby under certain conditions a charge may be made, but the province of Nova Scotia was contesting this claim; it is still in dispute, but notwithstanding that, the federal government held back this $133,000. That to me, Mr. Speaker, bears the earmarks of rather sharp business practice, and I do not know that we should sit idly by and let that sort of thing continue without making a protest, and we do protest against it.

Did the province of
Nova Scotia or the provincial government request the federal government to send troops on that occasion?

The attorney
general of the province of Nova Scotia did, I understand, ask that troops be sent down there, but as I understand it, under the Militia Act, which governs this matter, before any responsibility can rest on the province, action must be taken by order in council, and no order in council was passed by the government of Nova Scotia asking that these troops be sent there. I do not think that the government of the day in dealing with the provinces in financial matters should deal with them in a strict and rigid' manner. I do not say that the government should spend money recklessly, but I think it should spend it generously so far as the provinces are concerned.
Away back in 1867, under the confederation pact, we lost a good many of our elastic sources of revenue. They were handed over to the

The Address-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
Dominion parliament, and we were granted a small- subsidy in order to enable us to cope with certain matters of local concern. For instance, we had! to look after the public health of the province, education, and highways. Turn your mind back to 1867 and you will realize that no person at that time could possibly conceive that public health service would have developed as it has done and would require the expenditure that it calls for to-day. At that time public 'health was not a very serious question. Science had not developed to the stage that it has reached today, and it was impossible to forsee the large amounts of money that it would 'be necessary to expend on public health. The same applies to education. With regard to our highways, no person ever dreamt at that time that highways would 'have to be kept up in the state in which they are maintained to-day. That was before the day of the automobile, and people were not thinking then of keeping up the highways in an efficient state for automobiles and tourist traffic. But these burdens were saddled upon the different provinces, and we were expected to shoulder them and make headway on the small subsidies that were granted at that time, although they have been increased, it is true, from time to time. Under the Duncan report we should have received the increased subsidy dating from September 23, 1926.
Back in 1867 we were partners in the purchase of lands in the western portion of the Dominion, and we gave those lands away freely and gladly to make up the other provinces of the Dominion, in order that the prairie provinces might be carved out; and it is a good thing that we did, because the west has helped to make this country great, But, Mr. Speaker, we expect something iii return. The Prime Minister said the other day that the suggestion had been made-I do not know whether it was at the Dominion-provincial conference or not-that the western provinces should not only receive back their natural resources, but that the subsidies should be continued to them as well. I am in full accord with that suggestion. If we are going to maintain any standard of civilization in this country consistent with modern day requirements and our advancement, in so far as I personally am concerned, I thoroughly approve of the provinces getting the subsidies as well as their natural resources. I think this question has reached the point where this government should deal generously with all the provinces of this Dominion. As I have already said, this government has the elastic sources of revenue which we have not, and it
is very difficult for the governments of t)he eastern provinces to make ends meet. I call attention also, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that in the Duncan report it is pointed out very clearly that there is no extravagance so far as the administration of the provincial governments is concerned; no one can point to any reckless expenditure made by any of the governments. The commission states that the local governments of the east, and I am sure this applies to all other provinces, are carrying on their administrations as economically as possible.
Now I come to another matter and that is the representation from Nova Scotia in this House of Commons. We claim, and I think quite properly, that we have been overlooked to the extent of one member of this house; in other words, we have fourteen members from Nova Scotia and we claim that there should be fifteen members representing that province. I do not think I can do better in this connection than to read the statement which was presented to the Duncan commission, which makes the matter very clear. I might remind the house also that this matter was brought to the attention of parliament last session by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), but so far as I know no action whatever has been taken by this government. If you will bear with me for a moment I will read the few paragraphs in the brief of the Nova Scotia government presented to the Duncan commission dealing with this matter:
The population of Nova Scotia increased from 1911 to 1921 by 31,499. Quebec's population increased at a relatively larger rate, so that tile unit of representation after the 1921 census became 36,283. Nova Scotia's representation in the House of Commons was therefore reduced from 16 to 14. The population contained 33,965 more than was necessary to give fourteen representatives, but because we had fallen 2,318 below the fractional part, not exceeding one-half of the whole number required to entitle the provir 'e to a member, our population to that exten! was disregarded, and we suffered the loss of one member. Nova Scotia could not retain its members, as Ontario did. under subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act, whereby no reduction can be made unless the proportion which the population of the province bears to the total population of the Dominion be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
It may be difficult to overcome an effect such as this, but it is a fact that there are 33,965 persons in Nova Scotia unrepresented in tile House of Commons, while there are in Canada, outside of the maritime provinces, ninety-six electoral districts returning members with less than that population within their bounds. The membership for Nova Scotia cannot be reduced below ten, the number of our senators. But if by the increase of population in Quebec our representation were lowered to this minimum, it would mean a
154	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
total reduction since Confederation of nine. This is a condition which is being rapidly approached.
Had the unit of representation, instead of being 36,283, been 36,125, a difference of 158. Nova Scotia would have saved another representative, and instead of having fourteen members in the House of Commons would have had fifteen; that is, if the population of Quebec had been less by 10,287 persons the unit would have been so reduced. By the British North America Act, section 51, subsection 2-
"There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number of sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained)."
Quebec is defined by this act, section 6, as follows;
"The part of the province of Canada (as it exists at the passing of this act) which formerly constituted respectively the provinces of Upper Canada and Lower Canada, shall be deemed to be severed, and shall form two separate provinces. The parts which formerly constituted the province of Upper Canada shall constitute the province of Ontario; and the part which formerly constituted the province of Lower Canada shall constitute the province of Quebec."
That is, the popidation to be taken is the population of the territory known as Quebec at the passing of the British North America Act. But the population of Quebec which has been taken as the basis for the unit of representation since 1900 is the population of that province as originally constituted, plus the population of the extensions made by chapter 3 of the acts of 1898. It is now possible from information at hand to ascertain just what population was counted in these added territories. for they contain all of Abitibi, the district of Labrador, and what is known as part of East Maine, all that territory north of the height of land, part of it being traversed by the National Transcontinental railway. In extending, the boundaries further in 1912 the territory then given to Quebec was excluded in considering the population for forming the unit of representation, but the population added by the act of 1898 is included.
A statement from the Dominion Statistician shows that there were 13.644 people in this area. These should not have been counted in determining the unit of representation. Excluding them, the unit becomes not 36,283 as used, but 36.073. This figure divided into the population of Nova Scotia 1921 gives 14 and a fractional part, exceeding one-half of the whole united number by 778 and entitling this province to another federal member. The representation in the House of Commons from Nova Scotia, as fixed by the Redistribution Act, 1924 (14-15 Geo. \. C. 63). should therefore have been fifteen members. The province was under-represented in the last parliament by one member and will be in the next unless immediate steps are taken to correct this error.
I think that explains the matter fully. We understood that the province of Quebec, as originally defined under the British North America Act, was to be the unit acted upon.

Instead of that, however, in the last redistribution other portions were taken in, other sections were added and the population counted, which changed the unit and thereby deprived us of one additional member. We feel that we are entitled to this and we believe that the government of the day should take the (natter under immediate consideration and see that we get justice in this respect, This question has been to the fore for some little time but nothing has been done, and I sincerely urge the government that no further delay be countenanced in this regard but that immediate steps be taken to redress this wrong.
For a moment or two I would like to speak with respect to the steel industry, which at one time in this Dominion employed 20,000 men. It is true that this was in an abnormal period, during the war, but under normal conditions this industry employed about
14,000	men. In Canada to-day only about one-half that number, or about 7.000 men, are engaged in this work while steel products are pouring into Canada from foreign countries and putting our own workmen out of employment, causing many of our factories to stand idle and bringing depression generally to industries which once thrived and helped to build up communities and1 the nation. It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker that the government should take seriously under consideration the question of the revision of the tariff with respect to steel in order to provide this industry with sufficient protection to enable it to exist and carry on. It seems to me that it is not only a crying shame but a disgrace to allow an industry which has been built up in a country entirely adapted to it, to fall into decay as has been the case with the steel industry in the last few years. I would urge the government, therefore, that when the budget is brought down this year some attention be given to this very important question.
Then I have just a word to say with respect to the fisheries in my province. There has been a commission investigating that industry and endeavouring to find some means by which it may ibe placed upon a more secure foundation than has been the case for the past few years. The report of this commission should be tabled with the least possible delay, and immediate action on the report should be taken as soon as that is done.
During the past few months there have been some rather conflicting statements made with respect to the implementing of !the Duncan report. I am not making any statement in this connection in any carping manner, or with the intention of criticizing or
15.5

The Address-Mr. Thorson
embarrassing .the government in the least.
I think I am expressing the minds of the people in Nova Scotia when I say that we are very thankful indeed for what the government has done in connection with the Duncan report, but we do claim that they have not nearly implemented that report in full, and that some statements made by a minister of the crown with respeot to the implementing of this report are somewhat removed from the actual facts. I refer to statements made by the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Yeniot) at different places in the maritime provinces to the effect that practically all the recommendations and suggestions contained in the Duncan report have been carried out. Now, Mr. Speaker, we of the maritime provinces contend that this is not an accurate statement of the facts as they exist. As a matter of fact a great many far-reaching and important recommendations and suggestions in the Duncan report, have not been carried out. We were quite willing last session-those of us who sit on this side of the house-to give the government ample time to formulate their policy and to carry out in their entirety all the recommendations contained in that report. But the progress made. I must say, has been slow. People in the maritime provinces are waiting, but the conditions down there are such that they are not going to wait for an indefinite period in order to have these recommendations fully implemented. I was rather astounded to read the statements made by the Postmaster General speaking at two different points-at Amherst and at St. John-with respect to what the government had done towards implementing the Duncan report. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the whole of the recommendations in that report should be implemented without any further loss of time. I am sure that we on this side have endeavoured to help the government in respect to whatever legislation was proposed in that report. We still maintain that attitude and we hope to do everything in our power to assist the government in seeing that these recommendations are carried out in their entirety. But may I point out that delays are dangerous, that great hardships are being worked on account - of these recommendations remaining unfulfilled. I hope and trust therefore, that the government will take immediate steps to see that these recommendations are carried out in their entirety.
I did intend to go into some further matters, but I see that my time has elapsed. In closing I want to thank the members of the house very heartily for according me such close attention during my remarks.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this parliament it is singularly appropriate that the address in reply to the speech from the throne should be moved in both French and English, in order that we may constantly keep in mind the equality of the two languages in this country. I sincerely hope that the tradition in this respect which has grown up since confederation will not be departed from in the years to come.
May I at the outset follow the example of those who have preceded me in this debate and express my admiration for the brilliant address delivered by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), and at the same time tender my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beau-bien) for the able manner in which he seconded the motion.
May I also add my congratulations to those that have already been tendered to the hon leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on the great honour which was accorded to him by his party. I am sure that we all join in the wish that the great talents of which he is possessed may be devoted to the cause of national unity and prosperity. If it should ever be his responsibility to lead the government of Canada may he bring to the discharge of that responsibility the lofty sentiments of service to which he gave expression at Winnipeg upon the occasion of his selection as leader of the Conservative party.
I do not intend to deal at any great length with that portion of the speech from the throne which deals with the prosperity with which this country is undoubtedly blessed at the present time, nor to attempt an analysis of its causes, except to say that in large measure it is due to the bountiful harvests that we have enjoyed during the past three years, and to remind this house that agriculture is still the chief industry of Canada and as such continues to deserve our first consideration.
I do, however, wish to say a few words with regard to the great mining activities that are taking place in the province of Manitoba. I will not repeat what the hon. member for Provencher said with regard to the richness of the resources that have already been discovered. A new era is commencing in northern and eastern Manitoba, and I venture to prophesy that the history of northern Ontario in mineral development will be repeated in northern and eastern Manitoba. In order to promote and regulate that development we in Manitoba must look to the Dominion of Canada, for we do not as yet have control over our natural resources. May I here exio6
The Address-Mr. Thorson

press the hope that the question of returning to the western provinces their natural resources may be settled in the very near future. We have already, and very recently, had an excellent example of cooperation in the manner in which the federal and provincial governments worked together in order to make possible the development of the Flin-Flon mine, and I sincerely hope that that cooperation may continue in the future.
Two suggestions have been made with a view to promoting and regulating mining development in Manitoba. The first of these suggestions is, that the present system of taxing the gross output of a mine should give way to a system of taxing the profits of the mine, particularly in the early stages of mining operations. This system is in force both in Ontario and in Quebec. It is a system to which the investing public is accustomed, and provided the necessary safeguards are set up for the protection of the interests of the public, it is urged that a similar system of taxation be adopted for Manitoba.
The second suggestion that is made has to do with the registration of documents affecting mining claims. Under the law and regulations at present in force, title to mining claims in the province of Manitoba is by way of lease from the Dominion of Canada. This has been the system in force since 1914, when the previous system of granting freehold title under a patent from the crown was discontinued. Under the present system provision is made for the registration of an assignment of any right or interest acquired under the provisions of the Dominion Lands Act, provided that such assignment is unconditional and its execution is satisfactorily proved. No provision, however, is made for the registration, after the issue of a lease from the Dominion, of any other document affecting mining claims. There is no provision, for example, for the registration of that very common form of agreement known as an option agreement. It is urged, and I think rightly, that this is unfair both to the prospector and to those who have the capital for mining development. It makes it very difficult for the prospector who has staked a claim, in respect of which he has received a lease from the Dominion, to interest capital in the development of that claim, for persons are naturally unwilling to buy a claim outright, without first investigating its possibilities, and they do not desire to spend large sums of money in investigation on the strength of an option agreement when that option agreement may be defeated by the registration of an assignment of the lease from the prospector to 
someone else. Under the present system the door is open both to fraud and mistake. The person who is investing capital in mining development is entitled to certainty of title when he decides, if he should so decide, to exercise the option which he has taken. It is therefore suggested that provision should be made for the registration of all documents affecting mining claims either by way of amending section 86 of the Dominion Lands Act or by appropriate regulations. These two suggestions which I make have the strong support of the mining bureau of the Winnipeg Board of Trade, the Manitoba branch of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, and the Manitoba Chamber of Mines. Furthermore, the Manitoba government is in hearty agreement with the spirit of these suggestions. I therefore urge that they receive the serious consideration of this government for action during the present session, so that we may be prepared for the great mining activity that will undoubtedly take place immediately in Manitoba.
A moment ago I made the statement that agriculture was the chief industry of this country and as such continued to deserve our first consideration. May I add my voice to that of those who desire to see that industry promoted? The very small margin of profit which the farmers of this country make in the circumstances under which they operate at present, can be increased only by lowering the cost of production, the cost of living and the rates for carrying their produce to the markets of the world. May I express the hope that the burden of taxation, both direct and indirect, especially the latter, which now weighs so heavily upon the people and particularly upon the farmers of this country, will be substantially reduced during the present session?
Western Canada watched with a grdat deal of interest and with considerable alarm the investigations made by Mr. Palmer into the question of the Hudson Bay ports. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) deserves and has received the thanks of western Canada for the courageous and expeditious manner in which he dealt with this all-important question. In the larger field of international relations Canada continues to make progress, both in matters of trade and in the promotion of goodwill and mutual understanding with the nations of the world with whom she is associated. May I direct the attention of this house to the figures indicating the amount of our trade with Japan and China. The government is to be congratulated upon the manner in which it is facing Canada's international obligations. Canada has definitely ventured upon the wider arena of international politics. She is of the world and cannot remain outside it. Her representatives on the council will play their part in deciding the policies and exercising the executive functions of the league. As members of the council they represent not only Canada, not only the British nations of the world, but the total membership of the league, all the nations of the world that belong to it. to try and find means of alleviating the conditions that prevailed in the maritime provinces. We also had a commission appointed to investigate the administration of the Customs department. These are the main things in the estimation of the people of Canada. We have passed through that eventful stage of experimentation in legislation; those experiments have now become firmly embodied in the laws of our country, and the hour has come when the statesmen who control the destinies of our Dominion should solve these problems which will fit in with the growing needs of this great nation.
We have heard a great deal about immigration, but I say that in spite of what we have heard in this house, that we are making progress, no man dares deny that the greatest tragedy which could occur within any nation in the world is taking place every hour and every minute in Canada. We are losing the cream of our intellect; the youth of both sexes are leaving us, as regularly as the waters pass over the face of the earth, and they, are leaving us not to return. I ask you, sir, how this government is attempting to solve that vital problem, upon which the future greatness of this country depends. Is it right that to-day we should talk about plenipotentiaries, to foreign states when the very life blood

of our nation is ebbing away hourly and the government has not the ability or the machinery with which to check it?
Let me present to the house a few facts. I cannot draw a great dramatic picture, but by a simple comparison the smallest child may understand the situation. British Columbia is a country larger than Italy, Germany and France combined and to-day it has a population of about 560,000 people. New Zealand, a little country of 102,000 square miles, has a white population of 1,500,000 people and still, sir, the history of British Columbia antedates the political history of New Zealand. Let me show it in another way. The constituency of Skeena, which I represent, has a larger area than New Zealand. It is even larger than Great Britain and Ireland and yet to-day, with its fertile valleys, its millions of acres of land, its rivers, its seas, its mighty natural wealth of forest and mine, there are only 40,000 people to be found therein. Is there something wrong, or is it possible that I stand here this afternoon telling this house things are not existent? That is what is wrong with Canada. I felt that we needed a minister of finance who could demonstrate that it was possible for two straight lines to enclose a space and who could disprove Euclid's axiom that "things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another." In view of the fact that we are called upon to make very large expenditures-and when the estimates are brought down we will find that hon. members from all over Canada are asking for them, and there is room for increased expenditures-I can well imagine that the Minister of Finance will have a job on his hands to reconcile the two ideas.
But if we have not a minister of finance with courage, we have a Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) who at least has exhibited courage in his mode of dealing with the Hudson Bay railway. I think I ought to give him credit in any event for that. The easiest path for him to have taken would have been the path of least resistance, namely, to have gone forward with the development of the port of Nelson. In doing so he might have fallen back upon the reports of engineers who had previously given decisions in regard to the matter. But instead of that he took what at one time was an unpopular stand in this house. It was unpopular, I know', when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) took the stand that Churchill should be considered. Personally I must confess that at that time I took the stand myself that, unless very good cause could be shown for a change, having begun the development of the port of Nelson we should continue to develop that port.

We spent six million
dollars.

But in reading the reports that have come from Mr. Palmer I am satisfied that the correct decision has been reached. It seems, though, that we were formerly misled as regards the character of the Churchill harbour. I know I had always been given to understand that Churchill harbour had a rock bottom; that it would be impossible to
The Address-Mr. Brown

make a harbour there without a tremendous amount of work. The reports indicate that instead of the harbour at Churchill having a rock bottom it has a bottom that can be very readily dredged to make a harbour sufficiently commodious for the purpose in view. There was a disposition to establish comparisons between the engineers who years ago decided on Port Nelson and Mr. Palmer who has given his decision in favour of Fort Churchill. All I can say is that we have some little light thrown upon the engineers who chose Port Nelson when we remember that they sent up there a sand sucker dredge that never found any sand to suck. The nature of the bottom to the harbour would not permit of its being sucked.
I do not intend at this time to deal at any length with the tariff. Our position with regard to that matter has already been emphasized on both sides of the house, but I wish to point out one or two things with regard to the customs regulations of the day. I would like to endorse what the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Steedsman) said last night. The customs regulations are in some cases most annoying. I think hon. members and ministers do not always get the point of view of those who have to abide by those regulations. They should remember that over one thousand miles of the Canadian boundary lies between the great lakes and the Rocky mountains. It should be made as easy as possible for people living on both sides of the boundary line to obey the law. Customs laws are not very popular at any time. We all know that, but we should make them as easy of observance as possible. That is not the case at the present time. Indeed, a great hardship is imposed upon many innocent people who have to pass backward and forward across that line. I notice that in the report of the Customs commission there is a recommendation that the number of ports of entry be decreased. Before that is done, I would ask that the Minister of National Revenue give very careful consideration to the matter. I had hoped before speaking on this matter to have had the whole situation more completely in my mind as regards the number of ports of entry than I have at present, but I know that along my own line of railway within the province of Manitoba, which runs at distances varying from ten to twenty miles from the boundary, practically right through the southern part of the province, a certain number of customs houses and ports of entry are located. There are one or two others. I can conceive it quite possible to reduce the number situated along that line of railway 
without entailing any hardship upon any person. So far as the customs report deals with the merchandise brought in through those ports, I will take no exception to the recommendations, but if the number of ports of entry is reduced, account should be taken of the fact that it is not merely the merchandise. that actually comes in that has to be taken care of, but also the prevention of smuggling from the south, and further that reasonable facilities must be afforded those who want to pass backward and forward. If the minister carries out the recommendation without taking these considerations into account, he will make a mistake. I had occasion last fall to visit a point along the international boundary. I was asked to go down and see the condition of things that prevailed there, and I found that it was a matter of great hardship to the people who wanted to pass backward and forward to observe the regulations that were imposed as regards getting permits for crossing the lines and then the return of the permit. The character of the country there was such that men could not reach the nearest office without making long detours, and it puts honest law-abiding men in the position that they can only obey the law at very great hardship and cost to themselves. Before the report of the Customs commission is put into effect as regards reducing the number of points of entry, I hope this phase of the situation will be given consideration by the minister. The argument is frequently advanced in regard to the liquor trade, that bootlegging is increased because of the rigors of the law. Indeed, in the custofhs report, it is said that there would be less inducement to break the law if the excise duties were not so high. I am not going to discuss that argument in the meantime, but if it is true in regard to that matter, it certainly ought to be true in regard to the question to which I am referring; so that innocent people who want to cross backwards and forwards should have no more hardships than necessary placed in their way. We are aware that state roads are being constructed in the United States to meet the highways in Manitoba, to permit intercourse between the two peoples, and then we enact these very drastic regulations, to prevent the people making use of these facilities.
I shall not deal further with that just now but I wish to bring the matter strongly to the notice of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler).
I heartily endorse what has been said with regard to the necessity for the establishment of better facilities for promoting research.

The Address-Mr. Oott
Research i9 of importance to the farming industry because of the prevalence of and the destruction caused by rust. Indeed, unless some remedy is found for the rust that is now afflicting our crops there is great danger that Canada may lose the pre-eminent position it now occupies in the export of high class milling wheat, and no amount of money that can be spent will be too great if a solution of that problem can be found. If in attempting a solution of the problem we find it necessary to pay higher salaries to the technical men in question, pay them we must, and if in order to pay them we must to some degree upset the Civil Service Act, then upset it must be.
Hear, hear.

Because we cannot afford to lose the best trained men of Canada when they are needed to investigate these problems.
Mr. ECCLES J. GOTT (South Essex): Mr. Speaker, I should like to occupy the time of the House for a few moments to discuss the situation as it exists in western Ontario among the tobacco growers, which is most appalling. Before so doing I desire to join with other members of the house in offering my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Ilsley) and seconder (Mr. Beaubien) of the address, as I also desire to bespeak appreciation of the tobacco growers of western Ontario, particularly the riding which I have the honour to represent.
I desire to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), his deputy, Dr. Gris-dale, the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, Hon. John S. Martin, and his deputy, Mr. Roadhouse, for the personal attention they have paid to the tobacco growing industry of western Ontario. I desire to read an article appearing in the Tobacco Growers Guide, taken from the Farmers Advocate, which says:
The whole tobacco growing industry in Ontario is deep in the quagmire. The reasons given for this unhappy state of affairs are many and conflicting. Some blame the quality of the crop; others blame the tobacco companies. In spite of the British preference and the alleged demand in the United Kingdom, our tobacco is not moving and morale amongst the growers is at low ebb. When a situation such as this arises there are usually many reasons; and the only way to let in the light and clear the matter is for the growers themselves to be masters of the situation, know all the facts and through their own duly elected officers keep themselves informed as to requirements, values and movement of crop. So long as the growers know only the producing end of the business, and many of them knowing that poorly, there will be disappointments and failure. The only solution of the problem is a real business-like co-operative marketing company, owned and controlled by the growers themselves. Such a company could advise its members regarding acreage; through instructors it could assist growers in producing a quality product, and then it could explain to its members what the market situation really was. So far as Ontario is concerned the growers themselves would be masters of the situation and would not be working constantly in the dark as they seem to be at present.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the constituency which I have the honour to represent we produce approximately forty per cent of the entire crop of tobacco raised in the Dominion. During the last few months I took occasion by calling private meetings to ascertain if we could not uncover the discrepancies and discriminations that seemed to exist against the tobacco growers. I held sixteen private meetings before calling a general meeting, which was attended by seven hundred tobacco growers in the town of Leamington. These meetings were the prelude to a meeting that was attended by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and his deputy minister. Aside from the private meetings that I called, other meetings were being held in the county, and at one the following resolution was passed:
Whereas the farmers of Essex county have been induced by various ways and means to tremendously increase their acreage of tobacco and their capital investment to take care of the same during the past season;
And whereas these farmers are now finding that their marketing facilities, conditions and quoted prices are irregular and discouraging for the future.
The directors of the Essex County Farm Bureau request that you bring these conditions to the attention of your Department of Agriculture so that if possible we ascertain the reasons for these irregularities, with the end in view of having a more satisfactory solution found for this acute problem.
This was carried unanimously. In addition to those meetings there was a meeting of the tobacco growers of the township of Pelee island in the constituency of South Essex, and the following resolution was passed:
That this meeting, representing the tobacco growers of Pelee island, views with much concern the state of the industry, both as regards price paid by the buyers and the difficulties experienced in disposing of the crop to the best advantage.
We feel that the advantage of the British preference has not benefited the growers in any sense, but that the money has gone into the hands of the buyer, thereby depriving the grow'er of the benefit for which the preference was intended.
It is becoming obvious that the present state of affairs cannot go on, for the simple reason
The Address-Mr. Gott

that the grower is never sure of being able to dispose of his crop. Tobacco farming is not the easiest task in the world, and the grower wants to feel a little more confident concerning the disposal of his crop.
Having before us the wonderful advantage the wheat pool has given the farmer in the west, this meeting- is of the opinion that a pool, of a similar nature would be advantageous to the tobacco grower, and wishes to place on record its willingness to support any move made in this direction.
These are only samples, Mr. Speaker, of the resolutions that have been passed at meetings held in the riding which I have the honour to represent. Now, we have what is known as a British preference on tobacco. That preference was established by the British government in 1916 to induce the growing of better grades of tobacco in the British colonies for consumption in the British market. This preference was first given in 1916, taken away in 1921, and re-established in 1925. It gives the growers of colonial tobacco a preference of 49 cents a pound in the British market. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that if we had a higher tariff on flue cured tobacco coming from the United States part of the problem now confronting our farmers in the tobacco-growing sections of western Ontario would be solved.
May I direct, the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance to the three principal factors that enter into the solution of our tobacco problem? First, a more extensive cooperative marketing system; second, a reduction of the excise tax on cigars and cigarettes; third, a higher duty on flue cured and other tobaccos entering Canada from foreign countries. I think that the farmers are doing their very best to solve their present difficulties, and in - view of that fact I am going to ask the government to increase the duty on flue cured tobacco coming from the United States, not up to $1 or $1.50 a pound, but to 65 cents a pound. I think that will help to solve the problem. The Minister of Agriculture knows that it is a very serious problem. We have 5,000,000 pounds of the 1927 crop still unsold, in a non-competitive market, where there is no person bidding on the crop, and I think the house will agree with me that that is a very precarious condition for the tobacco growers of western Ontario to be in. During my investigation into conditions in the tobacco industry I was amazed to ascertain the profits of the Imperial Tobacco Company, and when I quote the enormous profits that are being made by this company, I want it understood that I am not taking issue with any director or any member of that firm. So far as I know, each and every person connected with the Imperial Tobacco Company is a gentleman; I hope so, at least, and every person who buys for them is, I believe, a gentleman of high standing. I am quoting these figures only to show the enormous profits that are made by the manufacturers as compared with those who grow the tobacco,
those who do the real hard work and suffer the hardships. I wish to show that the profits of those who do the real hard work are not all commensurate with the profits made by the tobacco manufacturers. Now during the year 1927 it is claimed that the Imperial Tobacco Company handled less than 10,000,000 pounds of tobacco. If that is the case, they made no less than 43.71 cents per pound on everv single pound of tobacco they manufactured. These are figures that have been cited not only at private but at public meetings. They are figures that have never been disputed, and I have every reason to believe that they are correct. The Imperial Tobacco Company or officials thereof also make enormous profits through the sale of fertilizer to the farmer; they get the farmer both coming and going. They sell the fertilizer at high prices to the farmer, and the farmer has to take any price they offer for his tobacco. It puts the farmer in a very disadvantageous position. He has to pay the highest price for the things he wants to buy, and when 'he goes to sell his products he has to take any price they offer. That of course applies not only to tobacco but to all the products the farmer raises in the Dominion. He pays the highest price for the goods he buys, and generally sells his products for the lowest price, due to the fact that he buys in a protected market and sells in a non-protected market.
I have before me reference No. 69B, which was an application made to the tariff board. Grothe, Limited, H. Simon & Sons, Limited, John McNee, Sons, William Ward & Sons, Limited, McLeod Nolan & Company, The Tuckett Tobacco Co. Limited. The reference reads as follows:

In making representation on behalf of the cigar manufacturing industry of Canada for relief from present taxation burdens, we would point briefly to the appalling decline in the past decade and a half. Further, we would again voice our contention that the increased duties imposed since 1913 were in the nature of war time levies and as such should now be removed.
The reduction in the number of cigar factories in Canada during the past ten years has been 60 per cent. Employment has been seriously curtailed; capital has been penalized and government revenue has suffered.
In order to restore the industry to anything like its former basis, material reduction in prices to the consumer must be made. Such a reduction is only possible through reduction of the levies which have been imposed on the cigar trade through taxation since 1914.
I heard two or three words of the speech of the hon. member who preceded me, and one word which struck me forcibly was the word "bootlegger." I want to say to the Minister of Finance that there is more bootlegging in the Dominion of Canada in the cigarette business to-day than in any other branch of commerce, and I will point out how easy it is to smuggle and sell American made cigarettes in Canadian stores. There are thousands of cartons of cigarettes coming into Canada on which no duty is paid. Across from Windsor there is a store at the foot of Woodward avenue in Detroit which caters to Canadian business. Men go in there and they are not content to bring a package of cigarettes across but bring two cartons on their hip, and if they are coming in cars they bring many more cartons of cigarettes with them. Some of the stores in Essex county import cigarettes and pay duty on them, but these are only sold when some officer of the law pays them a visit or when suspicious people are in the store. For the rest of the time they are selling cigarettes imported from the United States on which no duty is paid at all.
Cigarettes in Canada to-day are twice as expensive as in the United States, due to the excise tax. This brief also points out that the production of cigars in Canada has dropped from 294,772,935 in 1913, when the 28 cent and 42 cent leaf duty was effective with a flat excise of S2 per thousand, to 174,154,652 in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1927. I say to the Minister of Finance now that this reduction in excise which I propose will be' an inducement to Canadian manufacturers of tobacco to place on the market a cigarette which will appeal to the consuming public, and it will stop the smuggling of cigarettes to a very large extent. The excise tax on cigars and tobacco to-day is too high, and constitutes an extreme penalty on the consuming public, the manufacturer and the grower.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to place on record the imports of unmanufactured tobacco into the United Kingdom for each of the calendar years from 1922 to 1926 and for ten months of 1927, as well as the imports of unmanufactured tobacco into the United Kingdom for the fiscal years 1920 to 1924, which includes the importations from British Colonies as well as other countries. I also wish to place on record, with your permission, the exportation of unmanufactured tobacco from Canada by fiscal years for the years 1921 to 1927 inclusive. It shows that we have gradually increased our exports to certain countries, while in other cases our exports have fallen off. For instance, in 1924-25 we exported to Germany 794,815 pounds, while the following year we exported only 711 pounds, and for the year 1926-27 we exported 1,952 pounds. With your consent, Mr. Speaker, I will place these figures on record.

I desire for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the early vegetables which we produce in Essex county. I have the honour to represent the most southerly section of Canada, which I believe produces the finest crops of early vegetables in Canada. During the debate on the budget last year the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Young) made certain remarks in connection with the dumping clause to which I will refer. I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat, but I will read what he is reported to have said, which will be found at page 541 of Hansard for last year:
They told me that dumping was going on. I undertook to find out whether it was going on or not and to find out what evidence there was that it was being practised. I went to the Minister of Customs and asked him. He reminded me that the Liberal party was not in power at the time and that the Conservatives were responsible. He referred me to his private secretary. I went to the private secretary and he referred me to the deputy mfnister. I went to the deputy minister and he referred me to somebody else. I went to that somebody else, and he referred me to still another. I think I went to every man in the customs building, except perhaps the policeman and the janitor, and I put the same questions to . everyone. "What evidence had you that dumping was being practised last July when you imposed the dumping duty?" They all made the same answer: "Plenty of evidence",
The hon. member for Weybum used a good deal of space and a large number of words in explaining to the house that he was unable to find any evidence of the dumping of early vegetables into Canada during the year 1926. On July 1, 1926, I received the following telegram:
We respectfully wish to draw your attention to the fact growers here have been seriously handicapped by heavy importations of southern cucumbers and tomatoes which have severely

hurt marketing of our hot house crops in this district. We are now about to begin heavy shipments of field crops such as cabbage and tomatoes and if above unfair competition continues serious losses will be sustained by our growers. We would ask you to use every influence to remedy these conditions.
This telegram was despatched from Leamington and was signed by the Seacliffe Growers. That telegram was passed on to the Minister of Agriculture, who wrote me saying he had referred the question to the Minister of Finance, who in turn referred it to the tariff board, a body which I claim is inactive and never had many signs of life. On July 2, I received another telegram signed by the Seacliffe Growers, as follows:
Cabbage crop nearly unsalable. Prices offered would not net growers one cent pound. Tomatoes in much same position. All owing to import of American stuff which is being dumped in this country at prices that take such low duty that there is no protection to our growers. Cannot something be done to enforce anti-dumping act? This situation has already entailed serious loss to producers in this country.

During the week from June 24 to July 1 inclusive there were imported into Canada 128 carloads of tomatoes which arrived at their ports of entry practically free of duty, or at such a low rate that it meant no protection to our growers. When I returned to Essex county, from which the complaints had emanated, and visited the farms and fields, after ascertaining beyond question of doubt that the importations from the United States were causing serious injury to our farmers I forwarded the following telegram to the Hon. H. H. Stevens, who was at the time Acting Minister of Agriculture:
Vegetable growers of South Essex have drawn my attention forcibly to glutted conditions of their markets making it impossible to dispose of their produce with the result that crops are being left in the field. Government reports issued by the Fruit branch, Department of Agriculture, show hundreds of carloads of competitive vegetables imported weekly-see telegraphic report number 14 showing 414 cars imported into eleven Canadian centres during the short period of one week. During that period we exported to Great Britain $435,350,400 worth of products, and we imported from that country $227,000,000 worth of produce, giving a favourable balance in the case of trade with the mother country of $208,000,000. On the other hand we exported to the United States $477,154,614 worth of goods and imported from that country goods to the amount of $707,654,535, leaving an adverse trade balance with the United States of $230,499,921. Thus our trade with Great Britain resulted in a favourable trade balance of $208,000,000, whereas our trade with the United States occasioned us an unfavourable balance of $230,499,921, leaving us with a total adverse trade balance for the year of 22 million dollars.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the indulgence of hon. members for any imperfections they may observe in my attempt to present a few remarks in connection with the speech from the throne. Being a plain western farmer with no claims to oratorical ability and with but a very scant knowledge of parliamentary procedure, I trust their criticisms with regard to any observations I may make will be tempered with kindness, in return for which I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible.
In the first place I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) who made so splendid an address on Friday last, and also to make mention of the very able manner in which the hon. member for Provfncher (Mr. Beaubien) acquitted himself. I hope at some future time I may be able to present my remarks with the same assurance and ease of manner which my hon. friends displayed on that occasion. I also wish to congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on his having been elected to that high position, and, like many other Liberals present no doubt, I hope that he may long continue to hold that position.
I have been so much impressed by the grandeur and the splendour of these historic halls that I fear I may not be able to do justice this evening to my constituents, conscious that I am surrounded by brilliant statesmen and gifted orators. I can only comfort myself by remembering that, unschooled and inexperienced in parliamentary lore, nevertheless, as I wish to assure hon. members, I am sincere in my desire to be of service to my constituents and to Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend. On an occasion of this kind I could scarcely forbear to refer briefly to the celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation, and I think the national committee deserve our congratulations on the very successful manner in which that vast program was carried out. I am sure this celebration served to create a deep interest in Canadian history and tradition, because no one could have participated in that celebration without acquiring a more comprehensive knowledge of Canadian history. The various departments of government, both federal and provincial, reviewed 
the progress of our country since confederation in their many publications and supplied a mass of information on our political and economic development. In addition to this the newspapers, private institutions, and many individuals, contributed a large amount of valuable information touching on various phases of our Canadian life.
I am convinced that the influence of the celebration on the children of Canada must have been remarkably strong. From coast to coast our young people were busily engaged in essay-writing competitions and oratorical contests on Canadian subjects, which must have revived and deepened their interest in the study of Canadian history. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) referred very appropriately last night to that particular part of the celebration when he commented on the way in which our foreign-born young people had participated in it. When we reflect that it is on the rising generation tha't the future of our country depends, the keen interest displayed by young Canadians was gratifying. The very atmosphere seemed to be filled with harmony and unity, and with a consciousness of the fact that the entire nation was listening to the grand carillon pealing forth our national anthems. The inspiring words spoken by our foremost Canadians .seemed to find echoes in the hearts of us all. All question of partisanship, all distinctions of class, race or creed, were pushed far into the background where we hope they may remain forever. I am glad that at this session of parliament, following as it does the great jubilee of confederation, there appears to be even in this chamber an exemplification of that harmony and unity so strikingly in evidence last July, because sometimes on reading Hansard in the past I have been inclined to think that at times there was scarcely sufficient harmony to go round.
In the year just past we have had some very distinguished visitors in the person of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, his royal brother Prince George, and Mr. Baldwin, Prime Minister of Great Britain. While we as Canadians are always glad to welcome a representative of His Majesty to our shores, we always feel particularly glad to welcome His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, as wherever he goes he carries a message of goodwill, and through his kindly and cheerful personality he has done much, I am sure, to strengthen the bonds of sympathy and common interest which unite the various units of the British Empire. The visit of Mr. Baldwin might be considered a reminder of the importance of our jubilee of confedera-

The Address-Mr. Bock
lion. I understand in visiting us last summer he established a precedent, as prior to that time no British premier had ever visited one of the dominions during his term of office. It is also interesting to recall that Mr. Baldwin was bom in 1867, the year of confederation, and the fact that he celebrated his sixtieth birthday on Canadian soil was rather a pleasant coincident.
I should like to place on record a few remarks with regard to the Hudson Bay railway. In this regard I think the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) is to be congratulated on the very prompt manner in which he acted in making his decision in favour of Fort Churchill as the terminus of that railroad. He did not hesitate nor allow the grass to grow under his feet after he received the preliminary report of Mr. Palmer, and though his prompt action in this matter was criticized to some extent by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), yet we all are aware that had he deferred action in order to await the approval of parliament on a matter of this importance, he would have subjected himself to the criticism of every energetic citizen of Canada, including probably the leader of the opposition himself.
I believe it is customary for a new member to refer to some of the outstanding features of his constituency, and in this connection also I shall endeavour to be very brief. The constituency of Maple Creek is situated in the extreme southwest corner of the province of Saskatchewan. It is an entirely agricultural area- adapted to ranching and wheat raising. The western half of the constituency lies within the area known as the Chinook belt, which is not always blessed with the average or ordinary amount of rainfall, and which is subject in the growing periods to those hot winds that sometimes sweep in from the southwest and destroy the crops in a very short time. Many of the farmer's in that area are in a rather unfortunate position. A considerable number of the original settlers have left and have located in other parts of the province where the rainfall is more plentiful. Many of those remaining will never be able to pay up the amount still owing on their pre-emption. It has been thought by some that if they were given an opportunity to file on a second homestead-the abandoned lands in that area being made available for this purpose, with the indebtedness cancelled -it might assist them materially to carry on. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) last night touched on this phase of the situation, as his constituency adjoins mine and many of the conditions there are
much the same as those in Maple Creek. I have been informed that some relief may be anticipated, an act respecting debts due to the crown having been passed at the last session. This would mean that each case would have to be adjusted on its merits, I understand, as a blanket policy would involve difficulty in establishing boundary lines; that is, if a certain area were segregated it would apply to all located in that area. The settlers in this area are a very good class of people and are deserving of some consideration in this regard.
You, Mr. Speaker, have no doubt heard of the bountiful crops with which the west was favoured last year. We had an unusually late spring, and with the almost continuous rainfall seeding was not completed until about June 1, and in some cases later. We had an abundance of moisture, and the prospect looked veiy bright. Then, a series of disastrous hailstorms swept over the country and wiped out thousands of acres of splendid crops. This was followed by frost and then by rust, and when the crops were harvested continual rainy weather delayed threshing operations. To aggravate matters, winter set in on November 6, much earlier than usual, and I would judge that in the western half of my constituency at least 45 or 50 per cent of the crop is still unthreshed, having been snowed under. A large percentage of the grain that had been threshed was of low grade owing to frost and rust damage, and the wet weather prevailing at that time caused most of it to grade tough or damp. So when we read in the papers about the glowing conditions in the west, we regret that those conditions do not obtain everywhere.
In this connection I would point out that I believe conditions would have been, much worse had it not been for the operation of the wheat pool, for I am sure we are all agreed that through our system of distribution by means of centralized marketing we have been able to secure a much better return for our product than we could have done otherwise. I think the splendid success of the wheat pool in western Canada to-day constitutes a demonstration of the benefits of economic distribution, for while it raised the price of wheat to the producer-it has been said by reliable authorities in the neighborhood of 25 cents a bushel-it did not increase the price of bread to the consumer. Possibly some of our hon. friends who are seeking an upward revision of the tariff might be able to reduce their cost of distribution in somewhat the same manner.
The Address-Mr. Bock

I have noticed' in the press recently that some of the experts engaged in rust research work in connection with the Department of Agriculture might be obliged to discontinue it owing to the remuneration not being sufficient. I think, Mr. Speaker, that if this branch of the department has any hope of solving so serious a problem as that of stem rust, we should see to it that sufficient funds are provided to enable the department to carry on in this very important research work.
I could not very well refer to the constituency of Maple Creek without making some mention of my hon. predecessor, Mr. George Spence, who was our representative in this house in the last two sessions of parliament, As an untiring worker in the interests of his constituents he had no peer. He devoted a great deal of his time to the promotion of railway branch lines. Indeed, most of his electors were very reluctant to dispense with his services as their federal representative. His work in relation to the establishment of the consumers' league is, I am sure, well known to us all. I might mention incidentally that the winning of elections was one of Mr. Spence's favourite pastimes. I believe in the past two years he has contested and won four elections. This is a record which, I think, will stand for some time to come. To follow in the footsteps of so energetic a man as George Spence-he is now Minister of Railways and Highways in the province of Saskatchewan-is going to be no easy task for me if I make any attempt to maintain the fast pace which he set.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, possibly I should thank the hon. leads' of the opposition for the fact that the Maple Creek seat was not contested in the recent by-election, and I can afford to do so. But I am inclined to think that my acclamation was not due so much to any generosity on the part of the hon. leader of the opposition, or to any great personal merit of my own, but that it was rather a reflection of the confidence of the people of my constituency in the present Liberal administration.
